result: A new sedaDNA record from Stóra Viðarvatn, Iceland, shows Salicaceae present at ~10,850 BP (immediately after deglaciation) and Betulaceae appearing ~2300 years later at 8560 BP. The chronology is based on five tephra layers with linear sedimentation rates, and DNA preservation is consistent throughout the record as indicated by stable CT values.
evaluation: Claims C16-C26 and C145-C154 provide comprehensive documentation of the new sedaDNA record including site characteristics, core recovery, age model construction, DNA extraction success, sequencing results, and taxonomic identifications. The tephra-based chronology is well-constrained, DNA preservation metrics are stable (C47, C150), and the delayed appearance of Betulaceae is unlikely to result from preservation bias (C48). The data are internally consistent and methodologically sound.

result: A revised age model for Torfdalsvatn places deglaciation at ~11,800 BP, with sedaDNA showing Salicaceae colonization at ~10,300 BP (1500 y delay) and Betulaceae at ~9500 BP (2300 y delay). Early pollen presence of both taxa likely reflects long-distance transport rather than local colonization, as supported by the absence of macrofossils during this interval.
evaluation: Claims C27-C43 document the revised chronology and multi-proxy comparison for Torfdalsvatn. The revised age model (C31, C39, C40) is based on recalibrated radiocarbon ages using IntCal20 and is substantially younger than previous interpretations (C38). The interpretation that early pollen reflects long-distance transport (C41, C54) is well-supported by the absence of macrofossils (C33-C35) and the delayed appearance in sedaDNA (C36-C37), which has local origin (C13-C15). The colonization delays (C42-C43) are calculated directly from the data.

result: Comparison of the two Icelandic sites reveals that Salicaceae colonized Stóra Viðarvatn immediately after deglaciation (~10,850 BP) but was delayed by ~1500 years at Torfdalsvatn (the oldest deglaciated site in Iceland). Betulaceae colonization was delayed by ~2300 years at both sites despite different deglaciation times, suggesting catchment conditions may control colonization timing.
evaluation: Claims C44-C54 synthesize the Icelandic data to identify colonization patterns. The immediate colonization of Salicaceae at Stóra Viðarvatn (C45) contrasts with the delay at Torfdalsvatn (C42), and the inference that ~1700 years was required for initial establishment on Iceland (C51-C52) is reasonable given Torfdalsvatn is the oldest deglaciated site (C51). The similar Betulaceae delay at both sites (C43, C46, C53) despite different deglaciation times supports the hypothesis that catchment conditions matter (C53). The pollen interpretation (C54) is consistent with the multi-proxy analysis.

result: Eight published sedaDNA records from the circum North Atlantic (Baffin Island, Greenland, Svalbard, and Norway) show variable colonization timing for Salicaceae (ranging from immediate to 2100 years after deglaciation) and Betulaceae (800-6150 years after deglaciation), with all data derived from cited studies.
evaluation: Claims C55-C90 systematically document the published sedaDNA records used for comparison. Each claim is supported by appropriate citations to the original studies (Crump et al. 2019, Epp et al. 2015, Voldstad et al. 2020, Alsos et al. 2016b, 2022, ter Schure et al. 2021, Rijal et al. 2021). The authors appropriately note interpretive decisions (e.g., C65, C83, C87) and account for complications like marine inundation (C57, C64). This represents a thorough compilation of existing data.

result: Across all 10 North Atlantic sites, Salicaceae colonization shows no clear spatial pattern (immediate at 4 sites, 200-2100 year delays at 6 sites), while Betulaceae colonization is consistently delayed (800-5500 years relative to Salicaceae, 800-6150 years after deglaciation) with shorter delays at sites closer to refugia. Betulaceae only arrives during the Holocene at all sites, suggesting climate stability may be required.
evaluation: Claims C91-C101 synthesize the colonization patterns across all sites. The data are clearly presented in Figures 7-8 (C91-C95) and show consistent patterns: Salicaceae is variable but generally earlier (C92-C93, C100), while Betulaceae is consistently delayed (C94, C101) with a distance-from-refugia effect (C95) supported by dispersal theory (C96). The Holocene-only arrival of Betulaceae (C97) and the anomalous Langfjordvannet delay (C98) are well-documented. The climate stability hypothesis (C98) and soil development alternative (C99) are appropriately presented as interpretations rather than definitive conclusions.

result: Multiple biological and ecological factors explain the delayed Betulaceae colonization: (1) Salicaceae tolerates colder temperatures (bioclimate subzone A vs. D for Betulaceae), (2) Salicaceae has greater species diversity and environmental tolerance, (3) Salicaceae reproduces clonally while Betulaceae requires seed establishment with heavier seeds, and (4) modern observations confirm faster Salicaceae colonization of deglaciated areas.
evaluation: Claims C102-C121 provide a comprehensive mechanistic explanation for the observed patterns. Each factor is well-supported by citations: temperature tolerances (C102-C103, C105), species diversity and environmental constraints (C106-C110), reproductive strategies (C111-C116), and modern observations (C117-C121). The inference about dispersal probability based on seed mass (C116) is reasonable. The synthesis (C121) appropriately integrates multiple lines of evidence. The logic connecting these mechanisms to the observed colonization delays (C104) is sound.

result: Genetic data indicate Western European refugia for most Betula and Salix populations, with broad-fronted migration to newly deglaciated regions. Sea ice is a plausible dispersal mechanism for B. nana on Svalbard (Russian source), but wind and/or birds are more likely for Iceland, Baffin Island, and Greenland where sea ice was absent during colonization or source populations were in non-sea-ice-exporting regions.
evaluation: Claims C122-C136 integrate genetic data with paleoceanographic evidence to evaluate dispersal mechanisms. The genetic origins (C122-C126) are well-documented by citations. The dispersal mechanism analysis is logical: sea ice is viable for Svalbard given Russian origins and persistent sea ice (C124, C128, C130), but not for other locations because source populations were in mid-latitude regions that don't export sea ice (C131-C132) or because sea ice was absent during colonization (C134-C135 for Iceland). The inference about wind/bird dispersal (C133, C136) is reasonable given the elimination of sea ice as a mechanism.

result: The study demonstrates that Salicaceae can rapidly colonize deglaciating North Atlantic habitats while Betulaceae may be delayed by millennia, suggesting that future shrubification in deglaciating regions may be prolonged, potentially dampening changes in biodiversity, food web structure, and temperature amplification.
evaluation: Claims C142-C143 accurately summarize the main findings demonstrated by the sedaDNA data across all sites. The extrapolation to future shrubification (C144) is appropriately cautious ("may be prolonged," "at least temporarily") and logically follows from the observed patterns. However, the authors acknowledge uncertainty about applicability to non-glaciated tundra and note that baseline conditions differ between deglacial and modern tundra ecosystems, which appropriately limits the strength of the prediction.

result: Arctic warming at 2-4 times the global rate is driving shrubification, which alters tundra ecosystems and creates positive climate feedbacks through reduced albedo and increased water vapor, but the rate of future shrubification remains poorly constrained in Earth system models.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 establish the scientific context and motivation for the study. Each claim about Arctic warming (C1), shrubification (C2), ecosystem impacts (C3), and climate feedbacks (C4-C6) is supported by appropriate citations to the literature. The statement about model uncertainties (C7) provides clear justification for using paleoenvironmental records to constrain future predictions. This represents standard background material that is well-documented.

result: Traditional paleovegetation proxies (macrofossils and pollen) have limitations: macrofossils are inconsistently preserved, pollen is restricted to seed-bearing taxa and can be transported long distances (as demonstrated by exotic tree pollen in Iceland). SedaDNA provides improved reliability for taxa presence due to its local origin.
evaluation: Claims C8-C15 establish the methodological rationale for using sedaDNA. The limitations of traditional proxies (C8-C10) are well-documented by citations, and the Iceland example (C11) effectively illustrates the long-distance pollen transport problem. The inference about pollen not reflecting local colonization (C12) logically follows. The advantages of sedaDNA (C13-C15) are supported by appropriate citations demonstrating local origin and improved reliability. This provides essential methodological context.

result: Accelerating glacier and ice sheet mass loss is exposing new territory for colonization (1.7 million km² in Greenland plus >400,000 km² elsewhere), while warming will also enable woody plant migration across 5 billion km² of unglaciated Arctic tundra.
evaluation: Claims C137-C141 establish the future context and significance of the findings. Each factual claim about ice loss (C137), ice extent (C138-C139), and tundra area (C140-C141) is supported by appropriate citations. These claims effectively frame the relevance of the paleoenvironmental findings for understanding future Arctic change. This represents important contextual information but is not a primary result of the study.
